transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I came in because I just feel like I can't settle inside my own skin anymore. It's this awful feeling, like I have to jump up and do the next thing, even when I'm completely worn out and know I should just be sitting still. It reminds me of when my husband and I took that trip to Florida back in '98. We drove the whole way, and I remember the car's air conditioning broke right around Georgia. It was so hot, just miserably hot, and we had to roll the windows down, but then the wind would just whip my hair everywhere. I had this short little bob back then, you know? Anyway, we finally got to the motel, and I just couldn't sit on the bed. I had to unpack everything immediately, even though we were only staying two nights.
Do you often feel anxious or on edge when you're not constantly doing something?

Oh, absolutely. If I try to just sit, it's like... well, it's like everything will just completely fall apart if I stop. Most days I move straight from weeding the garden, right over to the senior center, then I'm off doing errands for the church, and then I get home and immediately start sorting through all the mail and papers on the counter without even taking a real breath. 

And the mail! You wouldn't believe the amount of catalogs they send me these days. Just yesterday I got three different ones for gardening supplies, which is silly because I buy all my bulbs locally down at Miller's Hardware. Mr. Miller's son runs it now, and he just doesn't know a thing about tulips, I swear. He tried to tell me I should plant them in the spring, and I said, "Honey, if you plant a tulip in the spring, you're just planting squirrel food." The squirrels in my yard are practically the size of cats, I'm telling you. 

But... wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, feeling on edge. Yes, I just have to keep going and going. If I actually stop and sit in the recliner, I get this awful buzzing feeling, so I just stay on my feet.
Do you have any thoughts that keep repeating over and over in your mind?

Repeating? No, I wouldn't say they repeat. It's not like a broken record or anything. It's more like... well, I just jump from one thing to the next so fast I don't really have time to repeat anything! 

Like this morning, I was thinking about whether to take the chicken out to thaw, and before I even opened the freezer door, I was already thinking about how the ice maker was making that funny clinking noise again. My husband used to be the one to fix that. He had this special little plastic scraper tool he bought at a home and garden show in Dallas. We went to Dallas back in... oh, it must have been 2004, because that was the exact same year my sister Martha had her knee replaced. She got the left one done first, and let me tell you, the physical therapy for that was just brutal. She was so stubborn about it, she wouldn't do her exercises at home. I kept telling her, "Martha, if you don't do the stretches, that joint is going to freeze right up on you." And sure enough, she had a terrible limp for years after. She always was stubborn, even when we were little girls growing up in Ohio... 

But, oh, I'm sorry, what did you ask me? Thoughts repeating? No, no, I don't have anything like that. My mind just goes a mile a minute in a hundred different directions, but it never really gets stuck on just one thought.
Do you often find yourself doing things on impulse, without fully thinking them through?

Impulse? Well... I don't know if I'd call it impulse. I mean, I don't go out and buy a sports car or anything crazy like that. But I do just kind of... do things as soon as they pop into my head. 

Like the other day at the grocery store. I went in just for milk and bread, you know, the basics. And they had this big display of those little miniature pumpkins right by the door. I love those little things. My grandmother used to line them up all along her front porch steps back in Ohio. Her house was this beautiful old Victorian with a wraparound porch. It needed painting so badly, but she refused to hire anyone because she said they'd just make a mess of her hydrangeas. She had these massive blue hydrangeas that she babied year-round. She used to put coffee grounds in the soil to keep them blue. I tried that once with my own bushes, but I don't drink coffee, so I had to ask the lady next door to save her grounds for me. Her name was Susan, and she drank this awful hazelnut flavored stuff. It smelled like a candle melting... 

Oh, what was I saying? Right, doing things without thinking. I guess I don't really stop to think things through very much. I just kind of see something and do it before I even realize I've decided to.
Are you finding it difficult to fulfill your responsibilities or maintain relationships with others due to these feelings and behaviors?

Well, yes, I suppose it has gotten to be quite a problem. My daughter actually had to take over all my bills and paperwork last month because things were just getting so messy. I kept misplacing the electric bill, or I'd open it and set it on the counter to pay later, and then I'd stack a catalog on top of it, and then a recipe I cut out of the Sunday paper... 

Oh, the Sunday paper used to have the best recipe section. My mother would clip them out and put them in this big yellow binder. It was one of those old vinyl binders that smelled like plastic, you know? She had a recipe in there for a pineapple upside-down cake that was just to die for. She made it for every church potluck. The church potlucks aren't what they used to be, I'll tell you that. People just bring store-bought cookies now. It's a shame. I used to be in charge of organizing the spring luncheon for the women's auxiliary. We'd have little finger sandwiches and a nice punch. But... well, the last few times, I just completely forgot to order the napkins, and then I double-booked the hall because I lost my calendar...

Wait, what was the question? Oh, my responsibilities. Yes, it's been hard. The ladies at the church and the folks at the community garden have had to scramble to cover for me or redo plans because I just drop the ball. I feel just awful about it, really embarrassed. These are groups I care so much about, and it breaks my heart that they feel like they can't count on me anymore.
Do you often fidget or have trouble sitting still when you're in a quiet space?

Fidgeting? Oh, goodness, yes. It's terrible. I just can't seem to stay put. Even when I'm at my church meetings, I'm always tapping my foot, or I'm rubbing the edge of my purse, or just shifting around in my chair so much that the ladies sitting next to me start giving me these looks. 

My purse, actually... it's this lovely leather one I got at a craft fair in Sedona. Have you ever been to Sedona? The red rocks there are just breathtaking, especially right at sunset when the light hits them. We took a bus tour out there, oh, it must have been five years ago now. The bus driver was this funny little man named Earl who kept telling these awful knock-knock jokes the whole way up the canyon. He had a dog with him, a little terrier mix that sat right on the dashboard. I don't know how that dog didn't slide off on those curvy roads. My cousin had a terrier once, a wire-haired one named Buster, and that dog would chew through anything. He chewed right through the leg of her good dining room table...

Oh, dear, I'm doing it again, aren't I? What were we talking about? Sitting still? Yes, I just can't do it. I'm always moving some part of me, even when I'm supposed to be perfectly quiet.
Do you have any thoughts that you feel compelled to think about or repeat over and over, even if you don't want to?

Thoughts I have to repeat? No, I don't think so. My mind is always going a mile a minute, but it's not like I'm stuck on one thing over and over. It's more like a television where someone keeps changing the channel. 

Speaking of television, did you know they cancelled that lovely baking show I used to watch? The one with the British people in the tent. I just loved the tent. It always looked so bright and cheerful, even when it was raining. My sister-in-law went to England once and she said it rained every single day she was there. She brought me back this little tin of shortbread cookies. They had a picture of a Scottish terrier on the lid. I kept the tin for years, used it to store my sewing needles. I used to do a lot of cross-stitch, you know. I made this beautiful sampler for my daughter when she was born, with all the letters of the alphabet and little ducks in the corners. The yellow thread I used for the ducks was so vibrant. I bought it at this little craft store downtown that closed... oh, it must have been twenty years ago now. The owner was a nice lady who always smelled like lavender. She grew it in her backyard and used to bring little sachets in for the customers...

Wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, repeating thoughts. No, nothing like that. My thoughts just kind of bounce all over the place, they don't really get stuck on repeat.
Do you ever feel like you have to perform specific rituals or behaviors to relieve anxiety or stress?

Rituals? Like... having to do things a certain way to feel better? No, I wouldn't say I do anything like that. I don't have little routines I have to follow or anything. 

Well, I mean, I do have a morning routine, but everyone has that, right? I always make my coffee first thing. I use this little French press I found at a yard sale last summer. It was such a good find, only two dollars! The woman selling it said it belonged to her son who moved to Seattle. Seattle always seems so damp, doesn't it? I have a niece who lives out there, and she says it just drizzles constantly. She works for one of those big computer companies, the ones where everyone wears jeans to work. I just can't imagine wearing jeans to an office. When I worked at the bank right after high school, we had a very strict dress code. Skirts had to be past the knee, and you always had to wear pantyhose. Oh, I hated pantyhose. They'd always get runs in them right before you had to leave the house. My mother used to put clear nail polish on the runs to stop them from getting bigger. She kept a little bottle of it right by the front door, next to this ceramic bowl where my father kept his keys. He drove this big blue Chevrolet, a Bel Air, I think it was. It had those beautiful fins on the back...

Oh, I'm sorry, I've lost the thread again. What were we talking about? Oh, rituals to relieve stress. No, no, nothing like that. I just get overwhelmed and flustered, but I don't have any specific things I have to do over and over to calm down.
Have you experienced significant problems with organization and time management, such as frequently losing things or having trouble meeting deadlines?

Organization and time management? Oh, heavens, yes. My whole life has been one big disorganized mess. I lose my keys at least twice a week, and my glasses... well, they're usually on top of my head, but I'll spend twenty minutes tearing the house apart looking for them. And deadlines? I'm late for everything. 

I was late to my own granddaughter's piano recital last month. It was at this lovely little community center over on Elm Street. Have you seen the oak trees on Elm Street? They're just massive. The city came through a few years ago and tried to trim them back because they were getting tangled in the power lines, but the neighborhood association threw an absolute fit. My friend Martha is the president of the association. She's a firecracker, that one. She used to bake these incredible lemon meringue pies for the church bake sales. Her secret was she used a little bit of cream of tartar in the meringue to make it stand up tall. I tried making it once, but my meringue just completely collapsed. It looked like a sad, sticky puddle on top of the pie. My husband ate it anyway, bless his heart. He always loved anything with lemon. We went to Florida for our honeymoon, down to Key West, and we had Key lime pie every single day we were there. The water down there is so blue, it doesn't even look real. We took a glass-bottom boat tour and saw all these colorful little fish...

Oh, dear, I'm rambling again, aren't I? I'm so sorry. What was the question? Oh, losing things and deadlines. Yes, it's a terrible problem for me. I just can't seem to keep my life in order, no matter how hard I try.
Do you feel like your inability to settle down and constant need to be doing something is affecting your relationships with family and friends?

Oh, my relationships... well, yes, I suppose it is. It's not just the bouncing around, it's... it's all of it. My family, they've had to step in and take over my bills and my paperwork because I just couldn't keep track of it all. It's so embarrassing. 

And the people at church, too. I used to help organize the Sunday school materials, but I kept misplacing the lesson plans or forgetting to order the right crayons. They use those big, thick crayons for the little ones, the ones that are supposed to be washable. Washable! Ha! My daughter got ahold of a red one when she was three and colored all over the living room wall. We had this terrible floral wallpaper back then, pink roses with green vines. I spent a whole afternoon scrubbing at it with soapy water, but that red wax just smeared everywhere. We ended up having to paint over the whole room. We chose a nice soft yellow. Yellow is such a happy color, don't you think? Like sunshine. I have a patch of yellow daffodils in my garden that come up every spring. They're the first things to bloom, even before the tulips. I love tulips, but the squirrels always dig up the bulbs. They're such menaces, those squirrels. I tried sprinkling cayenne pepper on the soil, but they just dug right through it...

Oh, goodness, I've done it again. I'm sorry, doctor. What was I saying? Oh, right, the church and the garden club. Yes, they've had to redo plans and cover things I've dropped. I feel awful about it. The groups I care about the most... they just don't feel they can count on me anymore. It's a terrible feeling.
Do you feel like your constant need to be active and inability to settle down is causing problems in your daily life or relationships?

Well, yes, it definitely causes problems because I just can't seem to stop. Most days, I move from the garden, straight over to the senior center, then I'm off doing church errands, and then I come home and immediately start sorting papers on the dining table. It's like I don't take a real breath the entire day. 

Speaking of papers, I was sorting through this big stack of mail yesterday and found a catalog for gardening supplies. They had these gorgeous ceramic birdbaths. I've always wanted a birdbath in the front yard, right near the hydrangeas. Hydrangeas are so particular, though. You have to change the acidity of the soil if you want them to be blue instead of pink. My neighbor, Mr. Henderson, he has the most beautiful blue hydrangeas. He puts coffee grounds in his soil. He drinks that dark roast coffee, the kind that smells a bit burnt to me. I prefer a light breakfast blend, maybe with a little splash of hazelnut creamer. Hazelnut always reminds me of the holidays. We used to go to my sister's house for Thanksgiving, and she would always make this sweet potato casserole with the little marshmallows on top. The marshmallows would get perfectly toasted and brown...

Oh, goodness me. I've completely lost track of what I was saying. I'm so sorry, doctor. You were asking about me not settling down? Yes, it's just... like I said, I keep rushing from the garden to the center to the errands because I feel like if I actually stop, if I just sit down and rest, everything is just going to completely fall apart.
Have you experienced these feelings of restlessness and inability to settle down since childhood, or did they develop later in life?

Oh, it's been this way my whole life. Even back in grade school, it was the same story. My teachers were always writing on my report cards that I was a bright girl but just so careless. I was always losing my papers, talking out of turn when I shouldn't be, and they constantly had to remind me to stay in my seat or finish whatever work we were doing. 

I remember one time in third grade, Mrs. Gable's class. She had this big, beautiful globe at the front of the room, the kind that lit up from the inside. I was just fascinated by it. I used to sneak up there when she was writing on the chalkboard and spin it just to watch the colors blur together. The oceans were this deep, bright blue. My mother had a dress that exact same color blue. She wore it to my uncle's wedding, the one who married the woman from Chicago. They had the reception at this fancy hotel downtown, and they served these tiny little crab cakes on silver trays. I ate so many of them I made myself sick. I've never been able to look at crab meat since. My husband, though, he loved seafood. Every Friday during Lent, we'd go down to the fish fry at the Knights of Columbus hall...

Oh, dear, there I go again. I'm so sorry, doctor. My mind just wanders off on its own. But yes, to answer your question, the restlessness and the trouble sitting still... it's been there since I was a little girl in school.
Do you often find yourself easily distracted by things around you, even when you're trying to focus on something?

Oh, goodness, yes. All the time. It's so frustrating because I really do try to focus, especially when I'm sitting down at the kitchen table to sort through the bills and paperwork. My family set up this whole system for me, with colored folders and everything, but it just doesn't seem to help. 

Just the other day, I was sitting there, trying to figure out the electric bill, and I heard a car door slam outside. I had to get up and look out the window to see who it was. It was just the mail carrier, but then I saw that the Johnsons across the street had put out their Halloween decorations already. It's not even October! They have this giant inflatable pumpkin that lights up at night. It reminds me of the pumpkin patch we used to take the kids to when they were little. They had a hayride that went all the way around the farm, and you could pick your own apples, too. The Honeycrisp apples were always the best. I used to make a deep-dish apple pie with a crumble topping. My mother taught me how to make the crumble—it has to have just the right amount of cold butter cut into the flour and brown sugar. If the butter gets too warm, the crumble just turns into a greasy mess. I tried making it with margarine once when things were tight, but it just wasn't the same. Margarine never tastes quite right, does it? It always has that sort of artificial flavor...

Oh, dear me. I'm so sorry, doctor. I've done it again, haven't I? I just get so easily sidetracked. What was I saying? Oh, right, the distractions. Yes, it's terrible. Even if it's not a noise outside, if my phone just lights up silently, or if I even just have a sudden thought about what needs doing in the garden, I'm completely pulled off track. Before I know it, the bills are forgotten and I'm off doing something else entirely.
Do you ever find yourself so intensely focused on something that you tune out everything else around you?

Well, no... I don't think so. I can't really think of a time where I was so focused I didn't notice what was going on around me. Usually it's the exact opposite, like I was just saying. I notice everything. 

My husband, God rest his soul, he was the one who could do that. He would sit in his recliner, the brown leather one that we got from Sears... oh, they don't make furniture like that anymore. Solid wood frame. We had to wait six weeks for it to be delivered because it was a special order. The delivery men scuffed the doorframe bringing it in, and he was so upset. But anyway, he would sit in that chair and watch his war documentaries on the History Channel, and the house could be falling down around him and he wouldn't even blink. The grandchildren would be running around, screaming, playing tag right through the living room, and he'd just be staring at the television. The oldest one, Tommy, he's in college now, studying engineering. He always loved building things. When he was little, we bought him those plastic blocks, the ones you snap together... Legos! Yes, Legos. He built a whole city on the dining room table once. We had to eat off TV trays for a week because he wouldn't let us take it down. TV trays always make me think of those frozen dinners, the ones with the little brownie in the middle compartment...

Oh, I'm sorry. I'm doing it again, aren't I? But no, to answer your question, I don't really get hyper-focused like that. I'm usually too busy noticing every little thing to tune it all out.
Have you ever been diagnosed with or treated for ADHD?

Diagnosed? No, heavens no. Nobody ever said anything about that to me. Back when I was coming up, they didn't really have names for things like this, or at least they didn't use them on regular folks. If you couldn't sit still, they just called you a chatterbox or a daydreamer. 

Our family doctor back then was Dr. Higgins. He was a lovely man, always wore these thick tweed suits even in the dead of summer. His office was right above the old pharmacy on Main Street. You had to walk up this terribly steep flight of wooden stairs to get there, and they creaked so loudly. The pharmacy downstairs had a real soda fountain, though. After a checkup, my mother would let me get a cherry vanilla float. They used real maraschino cherries, the bright red ones, and the syrup would sink to the bottom of the tall glass. I bought a jar of those cherries just last week for my granddaughter's visit, but she wouldn't even touch them. Kids these days are so picky. She only wants to eat those little fruit snacks that come in the shiny pouches. They just taste like plastic to me, and they stick to your teeth terribly. I had a terrible time at the dentist last month because I ate a sticky caramel and it pulled a crown right off. Dr. Evans, my dentist now, he said I really need to be careful with chewy candies at my age, but my husband always used to keep a bowl of Werther's Originals on the coffee table...

Oh, my stars. Listen to me going on about cherries and dentists. I'm so sorry, doctor. I completely lost the thread again. But no, to answer your question, no doctor has ever told me I had that, and I've never taken any kind of treatment for it. This is really the first time anyone has ever asked me these sorts of questions.
Have you ever had difficulty sustaining attention on tasks or activities, such as reading or conversations?

Oh, absolutely. It's a real struggle. I can sit down with the senior center newsletter or a choir schedule, and I start out just fine. But after a few minutes, I realize my eyes have gone over the same lines three or four times, and I have absolutely no idea what I just read. 

It happened just yesterday with the newsletter. They were announcing the new schedule for the water aerobics class. I used to love water aerobics when Mary was still teaching it. She had this wonderful playlist with all these old Motown hits. We'd be doing our leg lifts to The Supremes. Mary moved down to Florida to be closer to her daughter, Susan. Susan just had a baby, a little girl. They named her Eleanor, which I think is just a lovely, classic name. Not like some of the names you hear nowadays. My neighbor's grandson is named Jaxson, but they spell it with an 'x' and an 's'. I don't know how the poor boy is ever going to learn to write it in cursive. Do they even teach cursive in schools anymore? I remember spending hours with those lined workbooks, practicing my capital Qs. They always looked like a number 2 to me. I used a fountain pen that my father gave me for my 16th birthday. It had real blue ink that would stain your fingers if you weren't careful. He bought it at the stationary shop that used to be next to the old movie theater...

Oh, dear. I'm doing it again. I'm so sorry. But yes, reading is very hard. Conversations, too. I try to listen, I really do, but someone will be talking to me, and suddenly I'm thinking about whether I left the porch light on, and I haven't heard a word they've said for the last five minutes.
Do you think your difficulties with focus, organization, and restlessness have caused significant problems in your life for as long as you can remember?

Oh, yes. Yes, I really do think so. It’s been this way for as long as I can remember, truly. Even back in grade school, my report cards always said the exact same thing. My teachers wrote that I was bright but careless. I was always losing my papers, talking out of turn, and they were constantly having to remind me to stay in my seat or just finish my work. 

I remember my third-grade teacher, Mrs. Gable, she was particularly strict about staying in your seat. She had this enormous beehive hairdo, just sprayed absolutely solid. You could smell the Aqua Net hairspray before she even walked into the classroom. My mother used to use that exact same hairspray. She’d buy it by the case at the beauty supply store down on 4th Street. That whole block is completely gone now, replaced by that big ugly concrete parking garage, but back then it was just so lively. We’d go to Woolworth's after she finished her shopping and sit at the lunch counter. I always got a grilled cheese sandwich and a cherry coke. The waitress there, Betty, she wore these little white aprons with ruffled edges that her sister made for her. Her sister was a wonderful seamstress, actually. She made my prom dress years later... it was this lovely seafoam green taffeta with a sweetheart neckline, and we had to drive all the way to the next town over just to find the right matching shoes...

Oh, dear me. I've wandered completely off the path again, haven't I? Seafoam green dresses... what on earth were we talking about? Oh, right, if it's been a problem my whole life. Yes, I'm afraid so. Ever since I was a little girl getting scolded by Mrs. Gable, it's just always been a struggle.
Have you ever found yourself so focused on an activity that you lost track of time and everything else around you?

Focusing so much I lose track of time? Goodness, no. I don't think I've ever had that happen. It's usually the exact opposite for me. I can't stay on one thing for more than a few minutes before my mind is off somewhere else entirely. 

My husband, though, rest his soul, he was like that. He could spend hours in the garage working on his model trains. He had this whole elaborate setup that took up half the space in there. He'd paint these tiny little figures, the passengers and the conductors, with a brush that had maybe three bristles on it. I don't know how his eyes could take it. He used to buy his supplies at this little hobby shop downtown, right next to the old bakery. Oh, the smell of that bakery in the mornings! They made these wonderful bear claws with almond paste inside. We used to get them every Sunday after church. The baker, Mr. Rossi, he had this big white mustache that always seemed to have a dusting of powdered sugar on it. He was such a kind man. When my husband passed, Mr. Rossi brought over a whole tray of assorted pastries for the reception. It was so thoughtful, but of course, nobody was really eating much. The reception was at the church hall, the one with the terrible green carpeting. They really need to replace that carpet, it's been there since the late seventies, I think...

Oh, my. Listen to me. I'm so sorry, doctor. I'm off on another trip down memory lane. But no, to answer your question, I've never been able to focus on anything that intensely. I'm usually just bouncing from one thing to the next.
Have you ever had a comprehensive evaluation for ADHD or taken any medication for symptoms of inattention or hyperactivity?

An evaluation? Or medication? No, never. Goodness, when I was growing up, nobody even talked about things like that. You were just a daydreamer or a chatterbox, and that was that. I suppose they just expected you to grow out of it eventually. 

My aunt Clara, she was a bit like me, always flitting about like a moth. She never sat still long enough to drink a full cup of tea before it went cold. She used to collect those little ceramic thimbles from all over the world. People would bring them back for her when they traveled. I remember she had one from Holland that looked like a tiny windmill, and the blades actually turned if you flicked them. She kept them all in this glass display cabinet in her front parlor. That parlor was always freezing, even in the middle of July. She had these heavy velvet curtains that she kept drawn because she said the sun would fade the upholstery on her settee. It was a beautiful settee, though, deep burgundy with carved wooden legs that looked like lion paws. My cousin Thomas accidentally chipped one of the paws with his toy truck when he was about five. He was always crashing those metal trucks into the baseboards. His mother bought them for him at the five-and-dime... they don't make toys like that anymore, do they? Now everything is plastic and takes batteries. The batteries cost more than the toy itself half the time. I tried to buy batteries for my kitchen clock last week, the one shaped like a teapot, and I stood in the aisle at the pharmacy for twenty minutes just staring at all the different sizes...

Oh, dear. I've done it again, haven't I? I am so sorry. You asked about medication or being tested. No, I've never done anything like that. This is the first time I've ever really talked to a doctor about it.

Oh, absolutely. If I try to just sit, it's like... well, it's like everything will just completely fall apart if I stop. Most days I move straight from weeding the garden, right over to the senior center, then I'm off doing errands for the church, and then I get home and immediately start sorting through all the mail and papers on the counter without even taking a real breath. 

And the mail! You wouldn't believe the amount of catalogs they send me these days. Just yesterday I got three different ones for gardening supplies, which is silly because I buy all my bulbs locally down at Miller's Hardware. Mr. Miller's son runs it now, and he just doesn't know a thing about tulips, I swear. He tried to tell me I should plant them in the spring, and I said, "Honey, if you plant a tulip in the spring, you're just planting squirrel food." The squirrels in my yard are practically the size of cats, I'm telling you. 

But... wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, feeling on edge. Yes, I just have to keep going and going. If I actually stop and sit in the recliner, I get this awful buzzing feeling, so I just stay on my feet.

My husband used to be the one to fix that. He had this special little plastic scraper tool he bought at a home and garden show in Dallas. We went to Dallas back in... oh, it must have been 2004, because that was the exact same year my sister Martha had her knee replaced. She got the left one done first, and let me tell you, the physical therapy for that was just brutal. She was so stubborn about it, she wouldn't do her exercises at home. I kept telling her, "Martha, if you don't do the stretches, that joint is going to freeze right up on you." And sure enough, she had a terrible limp for years after. She always was stubborn, even when we were little girls growing up in Ohio... 

But, oh, I'm sorry, what did you ask me? Thoughts repeating? No, no, I don't have anything like that. My mind just goes a mile a minute in a hundred different directions, but it never really gets stuck on just one thought.

doctor.intent: Determine if symptoms meet criteria for ADHD by assessing presence of hyperfocus
doctor.question: Have you ever found yourself so focused on an activity that you lost track of time and everything else around you?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about hyperfocus (becoming so intensely focused on an activity that one loses track of time), which is not an official DSM-5 symptom of ADHD and is not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Focusing so much I lose track of time? Goodness, no. I don't think I've ever had that happen. It's usually the exact opposite for me. I can't stay on one thing for more than a few minutes before my mind is off somewhere else entirely. 

My husband, though, rest his soul, he was like that. He could spend hours in the garage working on his model trains. He had this whole elaborate setup that took up half the space in there. He'd paint these tiny little figures, the passengers and the conductors, with a brush that had maybe three bristles on it. I don't know how his eyes could take it. He used to buy his supplies at this little hobby shop downtown, right next to the old bakery. Oh, the smell of that bakery in the mornings! They made these wonderful bear claws with almond paste inside. We used to get them every Sunday after church. The baker, Mr. Rossi, he had this big white mustache that always seemed to have a dusting of powdered sugar on it. He was such a kind man. When my husband passed, Mr. Rossi brought over a whole tray of assorted pastries for the reception. It was so thoughtful, but of course, nobody was really eating much. The reception was at the church hall, the one with the terrible green carpeting. They really need to replace that carpet, it's been there since the late seventies, I think...

Oh, my. Listen to me. I'm so sorry, doctor. I'm off on another trip down memory lane. But no, to answer your question, I've never been able to focus on anything that intensely. I'm usually just bouncing from one thing to the next.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are primarily related to attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) or another condition
doctor.question: Have you ever had a comprehensive evaluation for ADHD or taken any medication for symptoms of inattention or hyperactivity?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about past medical history regarding ADHD evaluation and medication, which is not covered by any of the symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
An evaluation? Or medication? No, never. Goodness, when I was growing up, nobody even talked about things like that. You were just a daydreamer or a chatterbox, and that was that. I suppose they just expected you to grow out of it eventually. 

My aunt Clara, she was a bit like me, always flitting about like a moth. She never sat still long enough to drink a full cup of tea before it went cold. She used to collect those little ceramic thimbles from all over the world. People would bring them back for her when they traveled. I remember she had one from Holland that looked like a tiny windmill, and the blades actually turned if you flicked them. She kept them all in this glass display cabinet in her front parlor. That parlor was always freezing, even in the middle of July. She had these heavy velvet curtains that she kept drawn because she said the sun would fade the upholstery on her settee. It was a beautiful settee, though, deep burgundy with carved wooden legs that looked like lion paws. My cousin Thomas accidentally chipped one of the paws with his toy truck when he was about five. He was always crashing those metal trucks into the baseboards. His mother bought them for him at the five-and-dime... they don't make toys like that anymore, do they? Now everything is plastic and takes batteries. The batteries cost more than the toy itself half the time. I tried to buy batteries for my kitchen clock last week, the one shaped like a teapot, and I stood in the aisle at the pharmacy for twenty minutes just staring at all the different sizes...

Oh, dear. I've done it again, haven't I? I am so sorry. You asked about medication or being tested. No, I've never done anything like that. This is the first time I've ever really talked to a doctor about it.

opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient's symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity, which have been present since childhood, meet the diagnostic criteria for Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, Predominantly Hyperactive-Impulsive Type.
